dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: I say, Nikhil, don't you keep Browning among your books here? I was just telling Queen Bee of our college club. Do you remember that contest of ours over the translation of those lines from Browning? You don't?

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: I managed to get together the words to render it into Bengali, somehow, but the result was hardly likely to be a 'joy forever' to the people of Bengal. I really did think at one time that I was on the verge of becoming a poet, but Providence was kind enough to save me from that disaster. Do you remember old Dakshina? If he had not become a Salt Inspector, he would have been a poet. I remember his rendering to this day ...

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: No, Queen Bee, it is no use rummaging those bookshelves. Nikhil has ceased to read poetry since his marriage--perhaps he has no further need for it. But I suppose 'the fever fit of poesy', as the Sanskrit has it, is about to attack me again.

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: I have come to give you a warning, Sandip.

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: About the fever fit of poesy?

dialogue.speaker: Nikhil
dialogue.text: For some time, Mahomedan preachers have been about stirring up the local Mussulmans. They are all wild with you, and may attack you any moment.

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: Are you come to advise flight?

dialogue.speaker: Nikhil
dialogue.text: I have come to give you information, not to offer advice.

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: Had these estates been mine, such a warning would have been necessary for the preachers, not for me. If, instead of trying to frighten me, you give them a taste of your intimidation, that would be worthier both of you and me. Do you know that your weakness is weakening your neighbouring zamindars also?

dialogue.speaker: Nikhil
dialogue.text: I did not offer you my advice, Sandip. I wish you, too, would refrain from giving me yours. Besides, it is useless. And there is another thing I want to tell you. You and your followers have been secretly worrying and oppressing my tenantry. I cannot allow that any longer. So I must ask you to leave my territory.

dialogue.speaker: Sandip
dialogue.text: For fear of the Mussulmans, or is there any other fear you have to threaten me with?

Sandip.name: Sandip
Sandip.personality: Arrogant, manipulative, theatrical, insecure, prone to grandstanding, subtly resentful, enjoys provoking others.
Sandip.speech_style: Eloquent, verbose, sarcastic, prone to digressions and reminiscing, uses literary references to appear intelligent.
Sandip.description: A charismatic and influential figure, Sandip is a local leader who seeks to exert power and control. He is quick to anger and enjoys testing the boundaries of authority.

Nikhil.name: Nikhil
Nikhil.personality: Calm, rational, authoritative, observant, weary, concerned with justice and fairness, somewhat detached.
Nikhil.speech_style: Measured, direct, formal, avoids unnecessary embellishment, speaks with a sense of responsibility.
Nikhil.description: A landowner and the head of the household, Nikhil is a man of reason and principle. He is burdened by the responsibility of protecting his family and tenants.

Bimala.name: Bimala
Bimala.personality: Introspective, observant, conflicted, curious, somewhat passive, drawn to forbidden knowledge and experiences.
Bimala.speech_style: Quiet, observant, often indirect, uses subtle cues and gestures, capable of sharp retorts when provoked.
Bimala.description: The wife of Nikhil, Bimala is a woman of intellect and spirit, struggling with her place in a restrictive society. She is drawn to Sandip's charisma and rebellious nature.

context: Sandip, a local leader, attempts to provoke Nikhil, the landowner, with veiled threats and accusations.
